title: Crypto News Today: Bitcoin Loses $72K as $550B Vanishes From Cryptocurrency Market
summary: Bitcoin extended its November decline on Thursday, November 12, briefly falling below $72,000 as heavy liquidations, persistent ETF outflows, and renewed inflation concerns pressured cryptocurrency markets.
content:
Skip to content
Assets: BTC

Bitcoin extended its November decline on Thursday, November 12, briefly falling below $72,000 as heavy liquidations, persistent ETF outflows, and renewed inflation concerns pressured cryptocurrency markets.

The decline followed a broader deterioration in investor sentiment, with more than $550 billion reportedly erased from the cryptocurrency market since its October highs. Bitcoin’s latest weakness also raised concerns about whether the correction could deepen if institutional demand remains subdued.

Bitcoin Price Breaks Below $72K as Selling Pressure Intensifies

Bitcoin (BTC) fell to approximately $71,548, losing around 2.8% over 24 hours after retreating from an intraday high near $74,695. The decline followed a series of failed attempts to regain the $73,000 level, leaving the market vulnerable to further losses.

Bitcoin (BTC) price chart. Source: Brave New Coin

Trading activity showed BTC breaking below both $73,000 and $72,000 as sellers gained control. Data from Binance also showed Bitcoin briefly trading below $72,000 on November 12, marking its weakest levels since August, according to market reports.

The cryptocurrency later recovered into the $73,000 range, but the rebound did little to remove concerns about the broader trend. Bitcoin remained under pressure after losing several important short-term price levels.

The decline has also affected the wider digital asset market. Ethereum and other large-cap cryptocurrencies experienced selling pressure as investors reduced exposure to risk-sensitive assets.

Market estimates indicate that more than $550 billion in total cryptocurrency market value has disappeared since October’s highs. Bitcoin has also lost approximately 9% over the past week in the latest reported downturn, reflecting the scale of the correction.

Crypto Liquidations Exceed $650M as Long Traders Take Heavy Losses

Leveraged trading has amplified Bitcoin’s decline, with forced position closures adding to selling pressure across cryptocurrency exchanges.

According to liquidation figures cited in recent market reports, more than $650 million in crypto positions were liquidated over 24 hours. One estimate placed total liquidations near $723 million, with approximately 79% involving long positions.

Long liquidations reached $380 million in four hours, contributing to more than $650 million in total crypto liquidations over 24 hours, including $125 million cleared within minutes. Source: @BullTheoryio/X

The pressure intensified during shorter trading windows. WatcherGuru reported that Bitcoin’s drop below $72,000 triggered more than $125 million in long liquidations within 20 minutes. Another report identified approximately $222 million in long positions liquidated over 30 minutes.

Bitcoin futures traders also faced substantial losses. CoinDesk reported that BTC liquidations reached approximately $200.5 million over 24 hours, with 85% involving long positions. Total crypto futures liquidations surged to approximately $725 million during the same period, according to CoinGlass data cited by the publication.

These figures cover different reporting periods and liquidation categories, so they should not be added together.

The mechanism behind these events can accelerate market declines. When leveraged traders fail to maintain sufficient margin, exchanges automatically close their positions. These forced transactions can generate additional selling, pushing prices lower and triggering further liquidations.

The concentration of losses among long traders indicates that many participants were positioned for higher prices before the latest downturn. Their forced exits added pressure to an already weakening market.

Bitcoin ETF Outflows Weaken Institutional Demand

U.S. spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds have also contributed to the negative market backdrop. Persistent withdrawals from these investment products have reduced an important source of institutional buying demand.

According to CoinDesk, U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs recorded $95 million in net outflows on Tuesday, November 10, extending the withdrawal streak to four consecutive trading sessions. The publication reported that BlackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT) accounted for $78 million of those withdrawals.

A sharp market decline triggered $222 million in crypto long liquidations within just 30 minutes. Source: @WatcherGuru/X

The latest outflows followed withdrawals of approximately $201 million on Monday, $412 million on Friday, and $430 million on Thursday.

Together, these figures highlight sustained selling pressure across the spot ETF market. Other market reports have placed cumulative withdrawals above $1.4 billion over five days, although totals vary depending on the reporting window.

ETF flows matter because these products provide investors with regulated exposure to Bitcoin without requiring direct ownership of the cryptocurrency. Consistent inflows can support market demand, while prolonged withdrawals indicate that some investors are reducing their exposure.

The weakness has also coincided with pressure across technology stocks. Bitcoin’s failure to follow a rebound in Nasdaq-linked assets has raised questions about its near-term demand, particularly as institutional investors reassess their exposure to risk-sensitive markets.

Hotter US Inflation Data Raises Fresh Fed Rate Concerns

Macroeconomic uncertainty has added another challenge for cryptocurrency investors.

The US Bureau of Labor Statistics reported that the Consumer Price Index (CPI) increased 0.4% month over month in October, exceeding economists’ expectations of 0.3%. Although the reading was lower than September’s 0.6% increase, it indicated that inflation remained persistent.

Core CPI, which excludes food and energy, increased 0.3% during the month. Shelter costs rose 0.3%, while the food index increased 0.5%.

The hotter-than-expected inflation reading strengthened concerns that the Federal Reserve could maintain restrictive monetary conditions for longer or consider another interest-rate increase.

According to CoinDesk, traders raised the probability of a quarter-point Fed rate hike at the December 8–9 meeting to approximately 90% following the inflation release, based on CME FedWatch data.

Higher interest-rate expectations can weigh on assets such as Bitcoin by increasing the relative appeal of interest-bearing investments and tightening financial conditions. They can also reduce investors’ willingness to maintain leveraged positions in volatile markets.

CoinDesk also reported that stablecoin liquidity had weakened. CryptoQuant data showed that Tether’s USDT market capitalization declined by $6.6 billion over 60 days.

“Stablecoin growth funded every rally this cycle,” CryptoQuant wrote on X, according to CoinDesk.

A contraction in stablecoin supply can indicate reduced purchasing power available within cryptocurrency markets, although it does not independently establish the direction of future prices.

Bitcoin Price Faces $70K Support After Losing $72K

Bitcoin’s latest breakdown has shifted attention toward the $70,000 psychological level as traders assess whether selling pressure will continue.

The recovery above $72,000 offers some evidence that buyers remain active at lower prices. However, sustained trading below the previously established support levels could leave BTC exposed to another downward move.

Losing the $72,000 support level puts Bitcoin at risk of breaking below $70,000. Source: Monolith-Trades/TradingView

The broader market structure also remains under pressure. CoinDesk cited CryptoQuant’s estimate of Bitcoin’s 200-day moving average near $73,200, a level that has become important during the current correction. Its 365-day moving average stood near $76,400, highlighting the distance BTC would need to recover to regain that longer-term benchmark.

ETF flows, derivatives positioning, and macroeconomic developments are likely to remain important indicators of market direction.

For now, Bitcoin’s brief fall below $72,000, substantial long liquidations, and continued institutional fund withdrawals illustrate the challenges facing the cryptocurrency market. A sustained recovery would require stronger buying demand and improved market liquidity, while another loss of support could increase selling pressure toward $70,000.

title: Bitcoin Core Discloses Tor and Mining Bugs: Who Was Affected and What Was Fixed?
summary: New Bitcoin Core advisories detail three flaws fixed in 2025. The key questions are which nodes were affected, which versions contain fixes and what users need to know.
content:
Skip to content
Assets: BTC

New Bitcoin Core advisories detail three flaws fixed in 2025. The key questions are which nodes were affected, which versions contain fixes and what users need to know.

Bitcoin Core developers have disclosed three previously patched security flaws, including a Tor-related permissions mistake that affected thousands of reachable nodes and a high-severity bug that could stop an affected mining node from building blocks until restarted.

The immediate takeaway is practical: operators need to know which software and configuration they run. The advisories describe weaknesses in node software, not evidence that Bitcoin’s supply rules failed or that private keys were stolen.

Bitcoin Core Tor bug crossed a trust boundary

The Tor security advisory explains how incoming Tor connections could inherit permissions intended for trusted computers. Tor traffic reached Bitcoin Core through a local service. If an operator’s whitelist included that service’s address, outside connections could receive the same exemptions as trusted local peers.

Those permissions relax some denial-of-service limits and privacy protections. The consequence was a mismatch between the operator’s intended trust boundary and the connections actually receiving that trust.

The developers said the configuration led to “thousands of reachable mainnet nodes whitelisting all incoming Tor connections.” That describes affected deployments identified in the disclosure; it is not a current census of nodes still running vulnerable software.

Nodes that never enabled the non-default whitelist setting were not affected by this issue. The advisory rates it medium severity and identifies fixes in Bitcoin Core 30.0, 29.2 and 28.3, released in October 2025. The detailed public disclosure followed on November 10, 2026.

A separate flaw could interrupt mining

The high-severity advisory concerns what happens to pending transactions after a chain reorganisation. A reorganisation occurs when a node switches to a competing valid chain with more accumulated work, and transactions from disconnected blocks may return to its pending pool.

Under particular conditions, affected software could restore dependent transactions inconsistently. A mining node could then assemble a candidate block containing transactions whose required inputs were missing. Its own validity checks would reject that candidate, preventing successful block-template creation until a restart restored a consistent pending pool.

This was a failure in an affected node’s ability to prepare a block, not a mechanism for making the wider network accept an invalid one. That distinction explains both the operational seriousness for a miner and the limit of the disclosure’s implications for ordinary holders.

Bitcoin Core rates the issue high severity. The affected versions were 28.0–28.2 and 29.0–29.1. The disclosure credits Niklas Goegge with finding and responsibly reporting it in September 2025. It does not report an attack exploiting the flaw.

The third advisory concerns delayed block processing

A third advisory describes a separate way a malicious peer could delay an affected node’s processing of new blocks. Its severity is medium, and fixes were released in Bitcoin Core 29.2 and 30.0.

The concern is availability: a computer may be running but failing to keep up with the network promptly. For a business relying on its own node, that can complicate transaction monitoring and the timely interpretation of confirmations even without changing the ownership of any coins.

The advisory identifies conditions under which disruption could be repeated. Operators should follow the developers’ published guidance and use maintained software, rather than assume that a visible connection to peers guarantees the node is processing the latest chain correctly.

Why disclose bugs after fixes have been available for a year?

The timing follows Bitcoin Core’s disclosure policy. For medium- and high-severity issues on the standard timetable, detailed disclosure normally comes two weeks after the last affected release reaches end of life. The November advisories identify October 27 as that milestone.

That approach gives operators time to upgrade before a fuller explanation becomes public. It also creates an important distinction for news readers: newly disclosed does not necessarily mean newly introduced or newly fixed. In this case, the repair dates are in October 2025.

The policy now makes a separate provision for easily discoverable vulnerabilities, including flaws that can be found with minimal effort using an AI model. Such issues can receive a patched release and advisory as soon as possible. The three November 10 disclosures followed the longer timetable.

What Bitcoin users should take from the disclosures

For node operators, the relevant questions are version, configuration and operational dependencies. A package supplied by another vendor may bundle Bitcoin Core with additional software and settings, so checking only the name of the application is insufficient. The Tor issue shows why default assumptions about trusted local connections deserve attention.

For holders using a hosted wallet or exchange, these advisories do not instruct them to move funds to a new address. Their service provider manages the underlying infrastructure. The appropriate distinction is between infrastructure maintenance and a wallet-key compromise; the published flaws concern the former.

The subject is also separate from the longer-term cryptographic risks discussed in BNC’s report on Bitcoin public-key exposure and quantum computing. A software patch addresses a specific implementation weakness. Planning for future quantum capabilities involves a different set of protocol and wallet decisions.

The disclosures reinforce a familiar but consequential point: decentralised money still depends on well-maintained software. Readers can take the bugs seriously without mistaking them for evidence that every Bitcoin node was affected, that funds were stolen, or that the network stopped enforcing valid blocks.
